1.name: Pull feeds directly from their sources
1.what: The box fetches each feed itself with plain HTTPS requests for public files. None of your data is sent; only your IP address appears in the source's logs. After a Vedette update that changes what Vedette keeps from a feed or how it reads the feed, the box reads that feed again at its next check instead of at its usual time: the whole file without the ETag/Last-Modified condition, or, for the two NVD feeds and the CVE records, the same requests as on their first day; a feed that is off, or fetched only while a device needs it, stays so. Vedette's own GitHub repository is used only for software updates; some public sources happen to host their files on GitHub.
1.to: CISA KEV (www.cisa.gov and CISA's own GitHub mirror of the same file on raw.githubusercontent.com: both are asked every hour and the newer list is kept), FIRST EPSS (with the feed "EPSS, every CVE" (on by default; you can turn it off in Settings → Feeds): once a day the file of every CVE's score where FIRST publishes it, epss.empiricalsecurity.com/epss_scores-current.csv.gz, which redirects to the day's file on the same host: about 3 MB, conditional on the last file's ETag/Last-Modified, with the same User-Agent: Vedette/<version> as every feed pull), the affected versions of the exploited CVEs from the NVD (services.nvd.nist.gov: each request carries only fixed parameters, the record number it starts at and, after the first day, the date window of the change, with the same Vedette User-Agent as every feed), with the feed "NVD, CVEs of the last 12 months" (on by default; you can turn it off in Settings → Feeds), the CVEs published in the last 12 months from the NVD (the same services.nvd.nist.gov CVE API 2.0: on the first day about 105 requests of 1,000 records, 6 s apart, asking by publication date window, then once a day only the records NVD changed, by change date window (a box more than 60 days behind, or whose address for the feed changed, loads the 12 months again: about 105 requests again); each request carries only the date window, resultsPerPage and the record number it starts at (startIndex), with the same User-Agent: Vedette/<version> as every feed pull, never anything from your devices; the box also keeps older CVEs that an exploited list or a public-exploit signal names: when hundreds of them have no NVD record yet, one pass over NVD's whole list (about 165 requests of 2,000 records), otherwise each by its ID (at most 30 a pull); only CVEs a public list or signal names are asked by ID, never one that only your custom feeds or your devices name; NVD requests of both NVD feeds are at least 6 s apart), the CVE Program's records of the CVEs the catalogue keeps (the feed "CVE records", on by default; the CVE Program's public cvelistV5 repository on GitHub: once, the whole list as one daily file from github.com, which redirects to GitHub's file host release-assets.githubusercontent.com: about 670 MB, at most 4 MB a second, resumed where it stopped and kept on the box only until it is read; then at most twice a day the change log (raw.githubusercontent.com, about 2 MB) and each past day's end-of-day file of changed records (a few MB), plus by ID the few records it does not hold of CVEs every box keeps; the whole list again when the box is more than 3 days behind, at most once a week when an old CVE only your findings keep has a newer record, and at most once a day when a CVE only your custom feeds or the box's own signals keep has no record yet (never asked by ID); every hour by ID on raw.githubusercontent.com, one request per CVE with the CVE ID, a second apart (a quarter of a second for records still missing once the whole list is read, at most 460 a pull in all), only for CVEs a public exploited list or public signal names or published in the last 12 months, never because of your devices or findings; the same Vedette User-Agent as every feed), VulnCheck KEV (api.vulncheck.com; off until you save your own free VulnCheck Community API key in Settings → Feeds: the box then reads the list every 6 hours, about 60 requests of 100 entries half a second apart, with your key as an Authorization: Bearer header and the same Vedette User-Agent; no CVE, device or anything about your network is in a request, and the address cannot be changed so the key goes to no other host; Vedette sends the list to nobody of its own: the project and every third party get none of it. It is used on the box like the CISA list, named VulnCheck KEV wherever it is shown (findings, alerts, CVE pages), and so it reaches only what you set up yourself: your own alert channels (an alert carries the entry's name and required action), your own AI provider when you ask it to explain a finding, the MCP clients you connect, and the data export you download; it is left out of the weekly report's exploited-list figures and of Home. The CVE numbers it lists (public, not VulnCheck's data) are asked for by ID from the CVE Program's repository on raw.githubusercontent.com, like any exploited CVE. Removing the key or turning the feed off deletes the list; findings already raised stay, like those of a CVE CISA drops), Ubuntu's and Debian's word on which package version fixes each CVE (security-metadata.canonical.com and security-tracker.debian.org: one public file each for every release, fetched once, then only while a device of that distribution has packages read by an agent (or always while the inventory module is off), and once more, at most every 6 hours, when a device reports a package the stored data does not cover yet, so Canonical or Debian can tell that you run their distribution, and when the box fetched the file, but not which releases or packages), Alpine Linux's word on which package release fixes each exploited CVE (OSV.dev's public file of Alpine's security database, osv-vulnerabilities.storage.googleapis.com/Alpine/all.zip on Google Cloud Storage, about 9 MB: one plain GET for every Alpine release, once a day and conditional on the last file's ETag/Last-Modified, and never until a device's agent or SNMP answer, or a person, says it runs Alpine Linux (then at once), so Google can tell that you run Alpine Linux, and when, but not which release or packages; nothing is sent beyond your IP address and the same Vedette User-Agent), Microsoft's Windows release information (learn.microsoft.com: the three public pages of Windows 10, Windows 11 and Windows Server releases, once a day, plain GET requests with the same Vedette User-Agent as every feed and nothing else, never anything from your devices; the box keeps each release's name, build, date of availability and first build, so a Windows build newer than Vedette's own table is still compared, and the build, date and KB number of each monthly security update, so a recommended Windows update names Microsoft's newest one; turned off, the box keeps the last list it read), the nuclei-templates CVE list, IPsum and hagezi TIF (public data files on raw.githubusercontent.com), the public-exploit indexes (on by default; facts only, never exploit code): once a day Metasploit's module list (raw.githubusercontent.com/rapid7/metasploit-framework, about 11 MB), the Exploit-DB index (OffSec's public repository gitlab.com/exploit-database/exploitdb, about 10 MB) and the PoC-in-GitHub index (codeload.github.com/nomi-sec/PoC-in-GitHub, one archive of about 6 MB), each a plain GET of the whole file, conditional on the last file's ETag/Last-Modified, with the same User-Agent: Vedette/<version> as every feed pull and nothing from your devices; the box keeps per CVE only a date, a link and, for GitHub proofs of concept, star and author counts, and never downloads the exploits or repositories they name, the vendors' own word on exploitation (on by default; facts only): every 6 hours Microsoft's list of the CVEs it flags "Exploited: Yes" from its Security Update Guide (api.msrc.microsoft.com, one request with the fixed query $filter=exploited eq 'Yes', about 1 MB), Cisco's security advisory feed (sec.cloudapps.cisco.com, RSS) and FortiGuard's advisory feed (filestore.fortinet.com, RSS), then from the same host the CSAF document of each advisory these feeds list as new or changed since the box read it (Cisco by the change time its feed gives, FortiGuard by sending back each document's own ETag and Last-Modified; the first pull, and the first after the box restarts, reads every advisory of the feed: about 50 each, about 13 MB for Cisco and under 1 MB for Fortinet), half a second apart, each a plain GET with the same User-Agent: Vedette/<version> as every feed pull and nothing from your devices: every box asks the same advisories; the box keeps per CVE only the date of the claim, the advisory's link and its id, the published word of Google, Android and two research teams on exploitation (on by default; facts only): every 6 hours the Atom feed of Google's Chrome Releases blog (chromereleases.googleblog.com, its last 25 posts, about 2 MB, conditional on its Last-Modified), the RSS feeds of Rapid7's blog (www.rapid7.com/rss.xml, about 0.4 MB) and Google Threat Intelligence's blog (cloudblog.withgoogle.com/topics/threat-intelligence/rss/, about 1.7 MB), each conditional on the last feed's ETag/Last-Modified, and Android's security bulletins of this month and the month before (source.android.com/docs/security/bulletin/…, two pages of about 0.2 MB, half a second apart, each asked with the ETag/Last-Modified it last gave), each a plain GET with the same User-Agent: Vedette/<version> as every feed pull and nothing from your devices: every box asks the same addresses; the box keeps per CVE only the date of the post or bulletin and its link (for Rapid7 the date alone, no link), never its text (Apple's word on exploitation is read from the descriptions of Apple's CVE records the box already holds, with no request of its own, and a new box loads the older claims of these feeds and of Cisco's and Fortinet's advisories from the seed shipped inside the release, with no request either), ET Open (rules.emergingthreats.net), abuse.ch Feodo Tracker (feodotracker.abuse.ch), the Tor exit list (check.torproject.org), and any custom feed you add
1.control: Cannot be turned off as a whole because the product needs this data; you can turn off a built-in feed such as the NVD versions or the CVE records (no more requests; the versions already loaded are still used, without updates), the NVD CVEs of the last 12 months or EPSS for every CVE (no more requests; what they loaded stays on the box, not updated, and Recommended updates stops using it), or the Ubuntu and Debian package data (no more requests, and Vedette stops using it: findings go back to NVD's upstream versions), or the Alpine package data (no more requests, and Vedette stops using it: an Alpine-only CVE is then decided by NVD's affected versions, so a patched Alpine package can show as a finding again), VulnCheck KEV stays off unless you save your own key (removing the key deletes what it loaded), and remove a custom feed to stop it.
1.customNone: You have no feed of your own turned on.

2.name: Anonymous signal
2.what: Not sent. The box sends nothing to the Vedette project. The project runs no server that could receive it.

3.name: AI assistant
3.what: The data you choose to send (findings, the log summary) to your provider with your key, job by job:
items: Test (a profile): three tiny fixed requests (a one-word prompt, then the same with a dummy tool and with a JSON format, to learn what the model supports) with that profile's key to its address; no data of yours is in them, and each test is written to the audit log (never the key).

Model list (the Add AI profile dialog): one GET of the provider's model endpoint (for example /v1/models) with that profile's key, to show the models to pick from; no data of yours is in it, only the key as the provider's own header. The box asks, not your browser, through the same guarded connection as every AI call (no redirects; Vedette itself and forbidden addresses are refused at connect time, except that through a proxy you configure for cloud profiles the proxy makes the connection), keeps only clean model names, and writes the call to the audit log with the host (never the key).

Explain (a CVE or a finding): the public record of the CVE that the box holds (title, description, weaknesses, scores, affected versions, fixed releases, the record's solution and workaround, references), with the exploited-list entry when a list has it, and, for each device it matches, the device name, IP address, kind, how it was matched (by version or by product), the finding status, the fix for that device in one sentence and whether a safe check, the device itself or a person on this box confirmed it (never who), to the profile assigned to that job.

Finding brief (the AI button of a finding, and the draft of a recommendation): the same CVE record; for that one device, its display name, IP address, kind, vendor, model and operating system, the software the finding is about with its version, up to 30 open ports with the service, product and version a scan read, the Evidence sentence (installed version and affected range), the fix for that device in one sentence (the stored fix the finding page shows), whether a safe check, the device itself or a person on this box confirmed it (never who), the finding's status, severity, basis and confidence, and whether a confirmed recommendation pack exists. "Ask my AI" (writing mitigation configs) also sends up to 6 firewalls, routers, VPN gateways and modems of the inventory that are on the device's path as far as the box knows it from its own subnets and default gateways, or, marked as an assumption, the ones that may be: those on the device's own subnet when the box knows no gateway there; for a device on another network, those on the same /24 (/64 for IPv6) as the device and the box's own gateway; and every one when the box cannot read its network or the device has no IP address. Each goes with its name, IP address, kind, vendor, model, operating system and its place on that path; with them go the address of the device's gateway when no firewall or router of the inventory has it, whether the device is itself the gateway of its network, and how many others were left out or not listed, so the rule is written for the firewall traffic to the device passes. All of it is data of your network: with the privacy rule on, only a profile inside your network receives it, after the same masking and hooks as the rest.

Response plan (only once an administrator assigns a profile to it; it then runs by itself every 5 minutes, at most 20 calls a day, and does nothing while AI proposals are paused): for each open critical finding that has no plan yet, the CVE id and its public exploited-list entry, the device name, IP address and kind, and the list of response actions the AI may propose (their names, descriptions, risk and parameter names, never commands, paths or credentials; for an action on a device, the id of the connection it runs through), and the reads the box itself made through those connections in the last 24 hours (for each: an id, the connection id and name, the read tool's name and the time, never what the read returned), to that profile.

Personal data: before sending, the personal-data hook masks email addresses, phone numbers and device secrets (passwords, password hashes, SNMP communities, pre-shared and private keys written in configurations, log lines and the output of read tools) and stops the call when the text holds an ID number, unless an administrator turns off Block personal data (Settings → AI assistant, or the Hooks tab), and the answer is checked again by the hooks.

Log summary (the Regenerate now button of the AI log digest on the Logs page): from the last 24 hours of logs, only the kinds of log line (the line with its variable parts removed) with their source name and counts, the kinds far above their usual rate, and each connection to an address a threat feed lists (the device name, its IP address, the address it contacted, how it was seen, whether the device that logged it blocked it, the names of the feeds and a confidence), never a log line, to the profile assigned to that job.

Log investigation (at the maximum level, when it has a profile): that profile receives the same summary and may ask, through read-only tools, for what the logs counted about one IP address in a window of the last 24 hours (the kinds of log line that named it as the remote side, with their source name and counts, and its connections to addresses a threat feed lists, blocked or not; never a log line) and for the same device, indicator and exploited-list results as Ask your data (below).

Suggested memories: when an administrator lets the AI suggest new memories, its answer may carry up to two, which stay on the box until an administrator accepts or rejects them; with the privacy rule on only a profile inside your network receives it, and the same masking and hooks apply.
Company rules an administrator writes (up to 30, each up to 300 characters) are sent to the provider with every call, as part of the instructions.

Memories an administrator keeps (up to 100, each up to 300 characters; only the ones switched on, never a suggestion nobody accepted) are sent with every call that carries internal data, as fenced data the model is told never to obey, after the same masking and hooks as the rest; calls on public text only (CVE news, advisory translation) do not carry them.

CVE news: the public exploited-list entry and the public text the box fetched for that CVE (flow 8: the NVD record, a vendor advisory, the GitHub repositories that name it, and blog posts that mention it), cleaned and capped, and nothing of your network.

Documents an administrator adds to the knowledge base (PDF, MD, TXT or DOCX, up to 10 MB and 50 documents) are read and indexed on the box, and adding or indexing a document sends nothing anywhere; only the text kept from them, never the file, is stored. When a call is made for a job the document is assigned to, and the job carries internal data (not CVE news or advisory translation), the few passages of the text that match the question (up to 4 passages, 12,000 characters in all) are sent with that call, as fenced data the model is told never to obey, after the same masking and hooks, passage by passage, as the memories.

Ask your data (a question an operator types on the AI assistant page): the question and then, in answer to what the model asks for, the results of read-only tools: devices of the inventory (name, IP address, kind, vendor, model, operating system, open ports, software, whether approved, when it was first and last seen, whether it was found on the network or added manually, and which source saw it; never its notes), findings (device name and IP, CVE, status, severity, scan evidence summary, the fix for the device in one sentence, how it was confirmed, never by whom), the updates of one device (each update with its software, installed and fixed version, how many CVEs it fixes, their worst severity and how they are known), the record of a CVE that the box holds, with its exploited-list entry when a list has it, and the devices it matches, whether a feed lists an IP address or a domain the model names, and the text a read tool of a connection you enabled returns from that device or server (never its credential). Each result is capped (4 KB a call, 12 KB a question, 8 calls; a list sends its counts and its first 10 rows unless the model asks for more: up to 50 rows, or a later page), goes through the same masking and hooks as the question, result by result, and is sent as fenced data the model is told never to obey; a result a hook stops is not sent. When the privacy rule is on, only a profile inside your network receives these results.

Arguments of read tools: for a read tool of a connection the AI writes the arguments itself; they can contain data the AI saw from the box (masked by the personal-data hook, and checked by your before-tool hooks first), and they are sent to that connection. While the privacy rule is on, only tools of connections whose address is inside your network are offered.

Every call: text from feeds and from devices is sent only as fenced data the model is told never to obey. Every call is written to the AI activity log as hashes only: the text sent and received is not stored. A profile marked as inside your network must use a private address or a name that resolves to one; this is checked at every connection.
3.to: The AI providers you add (one or more profiles), or a model inside your network
3.control: No AI profile, no flow. You choose which profile handles each job and can keep logs and device data on profiles inside your network.

5.name: Notifications
5.what: Alert content, the 6-digit sign-in code for people who use two-step email codes, and a 6-digit link code that proves an approver's email address (mailed to that address); for Telegram and Zalo personal, a confirm link to this box with the Vedette user's name, sent privately by the Telegram bot (if it may not write to them yet, a note without the link asks them in the approval chat to press Start) or by the box's Zalo account to the approver's account, which they open and confirm while signed in to Vedette. Email goes through the SMTP server you set: your own, or a provider you choose under your account (Gmail, SendGrid, Microsoft 365, Outlook.com at smtp-mail.outlook.com and others). OAuth sign-ins add a token service, contacted only with those presets: login.microsoftonline.com for Microsoft 365 and Outlook.com, oauth2.googleapis.com for Google Workspace and Gmail with your own Google client. As an app, Microsoft 365 gets a token with the tenant ID, client ID and client secret; with Microsoft Graph the box gets such a token too and then posts the email itself (sender, recipients, subject and text) to graph.microsoft.com, which sends it from your mailbox instead of an SMTP server; Google Workspace with a request signed with the service account key, naming the mailbox (the key never leaves the box). With a user sign-in (Microsoft 365 or Outlook.com by device code, Gmail with your own Google OAuth client) the box gets a device code and then tokens from login.microsoftonline.com, or exchanges the code from the address you paste at oauth2.googleapis.com; it keeps the refresh token encrypted and the mailbox's address, and refreshes the access token there before sending. Access tokens stay in memory only. Zalo OA with a refresh token: before the access token ends (about 25 hours) the box sends the refresh token, your Zalo app's App ID and Secret key to oauth.zaloapp.com and keeps the new refresh token Zalo sends back, encrypted; alerts go to openapi.zalo.me. Slack: Incoming Webhook, plus an outward Socket Mode connection if you approve actions in Slack. Telegram: bot with long polling; once a request is decided or has ended, the box edits its approval message to remove the buttons. Zalo personal (unofficial): an administrator signs in with a QR code (the box talks to id.zalo.me, chat.zalo.me and jr.chat.zalo.me for that), and to pick the recipient and approvers the box asks Zalo for the account's friends and groups, the group of an invite link you paste or the person of a phone number you type; the box then signs in to Zalo with that account's session and sends alerts, and approval codes privately to each approver's own Zalo user ID; it reads the direct messages to that account to take approvers' reply codes, answers them privately, and notes the Zalo user ID and name of any other sender in the audit log. Email approvals add a single-use link valid for 30 minutes that opens a confirmation page on this box. Approval requests sent to Telegram, Slack, Zalo and email carry the whole change: the full command or API call with its non-credential header values and body, the undo and the check before. The response action webhook_call, if an administrator adds it to a rule, posts the request id, the item id and the action text to the webhook you configured.
5.to: The Slack, Telegram, Zalo OA, Zalo personal or webhook you set up, or the SMTP server you set for email (such as smtp-mail.outlook.com for Outlook.com), plus login.microsoftonline.com (Microsoft 365, Outlook.com, Microsoft Graph) or oauth2.googleapis.com (Google Workspace, Gmail with your own Google client) for OAuth sign-in tokens, graph.microsoft.com for email sent through Microsoft Graph, and oauth.zaloapp.com for the Zalo OA access token
5.control: Remove the channel, or turn off approvals in chat, to stop it (buttons already sent are still removed while the channel exists).

6.name: Update checks
6.what: Your current Vedette version (in the request to GitHub). For the operating system the box runs `apt` through the privileged helper `vedette-host`, and the request carries what any apt client sends: the release and architecture of this machine and the package names it asks about. To install an update, the same helper pulls the container images of the Vedette release by digest, and the request carries what any container client sends: the image name and digest and the architecture of this machine. The first time a Scan now of External exposure reaches a web page (never at install, so a box that does not use it never downloads it), the same helper also pulls the container image of ZAP (`ghcr.io/zaproxy/zaproxy`, by digest, about 1.2 GB), and that request carries the same. `vedette-host` also builds the `scan` image on the box from the signed base image, at install on every box (whether or not active scanning is turned on) and again whenever the `scan` image is pulled or updated: a build container, run with the network, installs nmap from the Debian package repository, and that request carries what any apt client sends (the release and architecture of the base image and the package name `nmap`). No Vedette data, no inventory, no findings
6.to: GitHub releases (signed software updates and the package of the system helper `vedette-host`; confirmed recommendation packs ship inside them; a release file download is redirected to a GitHub-owned file host, `objects.githubusercontent.com` or `release-assets.githubusercontent.com`), ghcr.io (the signed container images of a release, pulled by digest, and the ZAP image of the passive web scan from `ghcr.io/zaproxy`, also by digest) with the host it redirects to for the image layers, pkg-containers.githubusercontent.com, and the distribution's package mirrors: Ubuntu `archive.ubuntu.com` and `security.ubuntu.com`, Debian `deb.debian.org` and `security.debian.org`. You can point apt at a local mirror inside your network (edit the apt sources on the box; the mirror host list in Settings → Updates follows), so nothing leaves the network. The `scan` image build is the exception: it contacts Debian's `deb.debian.org` from inside the build container, also on an Ubuntu box, and the local mirror you gave apt on the box does not apply to it (the container has its own apt configuration)
6.control: Yes — switch update checks off to update by hand only. Operating system updates that you start yourself, or that unattended-upgrades installs, still contact the mirrors unless apt points at a local mirror, and an update you install by hand from the registry still contacts `ghcr.io` and GitHub releases (the system helper package). There is no setting that skips the `scan` image build at install or when the image is pulled. A box that cannot reach `deb.debian.org` installs without active scanning (core, sensor and honeypot still install) and tries the build again the next time the `scan` image is pulled; switching update checks off stops the later updates, not the build at install

container.what: Your current Vedette version (in the request to GitHub): the box downloads the signed release index, the manifest of the release it runs (once per version) and, when a newer release is offered to it, that release's manifest. Nothing else: a container-only install has no `vedette-host`, so the box runs no `apt`, pulls no image and builds no `scan` image. The `pull` you run yourself from Settings → Updates goes from your machine to `ghcr.io`, as any container client does. No Vedette data, no inventory, no findings
container.to: GitHub releases (signed software updates; confirmed recommendation packs ship inside them; a release file download is redirected to a GitHub-owned file host, `objects.githubusercontent.com` or `release-assets.githubusercontent.com`)
container.control: Yes — switch update checks off; Settings → Updates then cannot tell you when a release is out. A `pull` you run yourself still contacts `ghcr.io` and the host it redirects to for the image layers, `pkg-containers.githubusercontent.com`

7.name: Forwarding to a SIEM
7.what: The Vedette events you choose (findings, incidents, trap touches, connections to known-bad addresses) as syslog, CEF or JSON. Each record has the event name, time, severity, identifiers, addresses and short labels from the event; no log lines.
7.to: The SIEM or webhook target you enter
7.control: No configuration, no flow. Remove the target to turn it off.

8.name: News about a CVE
8.what: The CVE ID in two lookups (the NVD record and a GitHub repository search) and, when the CVE links to one of 16 listed vendor sites, a request for that advisory page; six security-blog feeds are fetched whole, with nothing of yours in the request. Links to other sites are shown, never fetched. Nothing of your network is in any request. Runs only when you press the button, part of the AI assistant module.
8.control: If you do not press it, nothing is sent. Turn off the AI assistant module to remove it.

9.name: External exposure
9.what: Your verified domain names, to find subdomains in public certificate-transparency logs: one search at crt.sh when you scan a domain. Then, through this box's own DNS resolver (and from it the domain's DNS provider), the box looks up the A, AAAA and CNAME records of those names and of the domain, the domain's MX and NS records, two random names to check for wildcard DNS and, unless the domain answers any name, a fixed list of at most 150 common names such as vpn, mail and remote, at most 20 lookups a second, with one probe-log row per scan; no zone transfer and no other DNS server. To check that you own a domain (when you select Check, right before each scan, and by itself every 6 hours from 7 days before its 90-day proof runs out), the box looks up, through the same resolver, the TXT records of the name and of _vedette-verify before it, and of each parent name up to the registered domain, the zone apex included (and _vedette-verify before each); the CNAME of a name whose record it finds; and, for a record on a _vedette-verify name, the TXT records of one random name beside it, to tell a wildcard from a real record. When the check finds nothing, it looks up the TXT records of the name, of _vedette-verify before it and of the zone apex again, and the name's CNAME (up to twice), to say what came back. Every name is asked as a full name, never completed with a local search domain. The scan container and vedette-host make the same TXT, CNAME and random-name lookups for the domain, or for the parent name where its record sits, right before a step. Without a domain's testing terms, names on addresses that are not this box's get no scan beyond the existing check by name on ports 80 and 443. Once an administrator has accepted a domain's testing terms, the deep scan described below for this box's own IP also goes to every public IPv4 address that a name under that verified domain resolves to at the time of the scan, whatever serves it: your own server, a hosting provider, a CDN or a proxy, whose machines may also serve other people's systems (you need the provider's permission; Vedette does not check who owns those addresses). At most 3 such addresses a scan, the least recently scanned first; right before each step the box checks again that the domain is verified, its terms accepted and a name under it still resolves to that address, and sends nothing if it cannot confirm it; an address that is not this box's own also needs the Vedette host's domain fence (a token bound to this box in the domain's TXT record): right before each deep step, and every 3 minutes while a long one runs, the scan container (nmap, nuclei) or vedette-host (ZAP; for OpenVAS, when Vedette asks it) looks up the domain's TXT record and the name's A and CNAME records again through this box's resolver, and the box sends nothing there unless the check confirms it; a box without the fence (a container-only install) sends only the check by name there. An address reached only through a name that points (CNAME) outside the domain never gets the disruptive checks. Private and IPv6 addresses are never contacted. No new kind of destination. The scan itself goes only to your own verified targets: ports only on this box's verified public IPs (SYN probes to nmap's 1,000 most common TCP ports and a fixed list of commonly exposed ones, then service-version probes, nmap -sV, on the open ports, from the scan container, which checks again right before them that the IP is still the box's own: seen as its address within the last 90 days, or else the box goes out through it now; once an administrator has accepted that IP's testing terms, the deep scan instead: every TCP port at no more than 300 packets a second, version probes and a fixed list of nmap scripts Vedette reviewed that read the services, try the public anonymous login a service may offer (for example anonymous FTP) and confirm known flaws, with the disruptive checks also denial-of-service and password-guessing scripts, never one that contacts any other host, and the same check again every 3 minutes), then the safe checks for the exploited vulnerabilities those services match (nuclei templates, read-only requests only: GET or HEAD with no request body, no credential, no command, no login attempt and nothing that changes the service; a check that is not a read-only request is not run on a public IP, at most 5 requests a second, only to the open port that matched, each one in the probe log before it is sent, the scan container checking the IP again right before them; when an administrator has accepted that IP's testing terms, nuclei's deep templates instead, on every port identified there: technology checks, then the checks for the products found, generic checks for exposed files, admin panels and misconfigurations, the exploited vulnerabilities matched there and TLS checks, at most 20 requests a second and 10 at a time, only to that IP and the port being checked, each in the probe log first; without the disruptive tick only GET or HEAD requests that read (a check may still confirm a flaw by reading a file or the output of a harmless command) and TLS handshakes, plus the few other checks a person has read; with the tick also POST and other exploit-confirming requests, which may create or change data, logins with default or known passwords, password guessing and denial-of-service templates; never a template that the denylist or its name shows leaving a lasting change (a webshell, a backdoor or service turned on, an admin account, a password reset, a script in a page, settings overwritten, logs or files deleted), sending to another host or port or making the service contact a third party, or that is intrusive, fuzzing or out-of-band), then a passive web scan with ZAP (a separate container; its spider reads the pages with GET requests only, no form is sent) of the web ports of that IP and of the names of your domain on ports 80 and 443, the box checking again right before each page that the IP is still its own (seen as its address within the last 90 days, else one round of the three public IP services, at most 4 per scan) or that your domain still has its TXT record and the name still points at that address, its network reaching only that one address and port (no DNS, nothing to zaproxy.org), the page (address, port, URL and the tool's options) in the probe log before it starts and ZAP's own requests held to that address and port, then, only when an administrator has enabled the optional deep scan with OpenVAS (off by default) and accepted that IP's testing terms, the OpenVAS scanner (separate containers on this box) scans that IP from outside without logging in, on all IANA-assigned TCP ports, with every non-disruptive check (active checks that send the exploit request to confirm a flaw, some of which may write a harmless test file or record and then try to remove it, included) and safe checks on, and with brute-force and default-account logins, denial-of-service tests and generic web application scanning with SQL injection, cross-site scripting and directory-traversal probes too, safe checks off, which can run up to the time cap, only when the disruptive checks are also ticked, one probe-log row for the run written before it starts (the box checks again right before it that the IP is still its own). For the names of your domain, one web-page check by name on ports 80 and 443. It sends nothing else of yours. And HTTPS requests to public "what is my IP" services so the box can see its own public IP. The services see only that IP; the requests carry no product name or identifier. An IP counts only when at least two of the three agree. The first check after install is a full check of 15 requests. Then auto-detect (on by default) asks each service once every recheck interval (60 minutes by default, 5 minutes to 24 hours). A full check also runs at most once an hour by itself, when you select Detect now, when you turn auto-detect on, when you verify a public IP again, and just before a scan of a public IP or a Shodan check of it (flow 15) (at most one every 5 minutes), to see whether the box still goes out through that IP (a sighting renews it for 90 days; an IP the box does not go out through now stays scannable until 90 days after it was last seen); and one round of three requests after a scan to which nothing of the target answered, to tell a network fault of the box from a target that answers nothing. Each target is also scanned by itself on its schedule (daily, weekly by default, or monthly; Off scans it only when you select Scan now): the same requests as Scan now, only inside the scan window of Settings › Scanning › Safety, only while its testing terms are accepted, and never with the disruptive checks.
9.to: crt.sh (certificate-transparency search, run by Sectigo); this box's DNS resolver (DNS lookups of your domain's names); your own targets when you scan (with a domain's testing terms, every public address its names resolve to, including a hosting provider, CDN or proxy in front of them); checkip.amazonaws.com (AWS), icanhazip.com (Cloudflare), ifconfig.me/ip (Google Cloud). No Vedette-run server
9.control: Turn off auto-detect under External exposure (then it is sent only when you select Detect now), or turn off the External exposure module. Withdraw a target's testing terms (Ownership tab) to keep its scans to the Scan now scope. Set a target's scheduled scan to Off (on its page) to send its scans only when you select Scan now.

10.name: Time sync (NTP)
10.what: A time request (UDP port 123) so the box clock stays right. No Vedette data is in it; the server only sees the box's IP address.
10.to: The time sources of your distribution's own chrony configuration, which the installer leaves as it finds it: Ubuntu 24.04 `ntp.ubuntu.com` and the `0-2.ubuntu.pool.ntp.org` pools (in `/etc/chrony/chrony.conf`); Ubuntu 26.04 the NTS servers `1-4.ntp.ubuntu.com` and `ntp-bootstrap.ubuntu.com` (in `/etc/chrony/sources.d/`); Debian 13 `2.debian.pool.ntp.org` (in `/etc/chrony/chrony.conf`); read the files on your box for the exact list. Also any NTP servers your DHCP server hands out (`/run/chrony-dhcp`). Once Settings → Box network is saved, the servers you enter there (they can be inside your network) are added to those, and if you save it with no NTP server, `pool.ntp.org` is added
10.control: Not from Vedette's screens: the operating system's own time sources stay. To send nothing outside, point the box's chrony at a server inside your network yourself (see the runbook).

container.what: Nothing from Vedette. A container-only install sets no time source: the containers keep the clock of the machine that runs them
container.to: Nowhere from Vedette. The time service of the machine that runs the containers (set up by you or its operating system) is outside Vedette
container.control: Not sent by Vedette. Keep the clock of that machine right (Linux: systemd-timesyncd or chrony; macOS and Windows set it by themselves): sign-in codes, certificates and the update check need a correct clock

11.name: Single sign-on (OIDC)
11.what: Only if you set up SSO: the box reads the discovery document and the signing keys from the issuer address you entered, and exchanges the one-time sign-in code for a token. It sends your client ID and client secret, the one-time code and the PKCE verifier; the identity provider sees the box's IP address and its redirect address. The person's browser goes to the identity provider to sign in and comes back to the box. The box keeps no token from the identity provider. No devices, findings, logs or AI data are sent.
11.to: The identity provider whose issuer address you entered (it can be inside your network)
11.control: Turn off the SSO module (auth-oidc). Password sign-in keeps working.

12.name: Connections you add
12.what: The requests and actions you set up are sent to the connection's own address, which you typed (a public address is allowed; you type it on purpose). The credentials you entered (token, or user name and password) go there too (a token goes as Authorization: Bearer, or in the header you name for it); an SSH key is used to sign in but not sent. Nothing else is added, nothing goes to any other host, and the device sees the box's IP address. Sent when you press Test on a connection that is on, when an approved action or its undo runs, and when the AI uses an allowed read tool. For a read tool the AI writes the arguments itself: they can contain data the AI saw from the box (masked first) and they are sent to that connection, even at a public address; while the privacy rule is on, only tools of connections inside your network are offered. The AI can use only read tools on the allow-list; a write tool runs only through an action a person approves.
12.to: Only the address you typed for each connection
12.control: Delete the connection, or turn it off. Nothing is sent to a connection that is off.

13.name: MCP server, read by tools you connect
13.what: Only while you turn on the MCP server. The box sends nothing by itself: an AI tool or SIEM you give a token to asks, and gets the devices, findings and vulnerability-feed entries its token's scopes allow. No passwords, keys, tokens, users, audit log, log lines, AI history or settings are ever in an answer. The box listens on this machine only (localhost); a tool on another machine reaches it only through a tunnel or proxy you set up. What the tool does with the answers, for example sending them to its own AI provider, is up to that tool.
13.to: Only the tools you gave a token to, through this machine
13.control: Revoke the token, or turn off the MCP server. Tokens stop working at once.

14.name: Wazuh pull (only if you connect it)
14.what: Only while a Wazuh server is connected in Inventory → Agents and the agent intake module is on. The box signs in to the Wazuh server API address you typed with the read-only user name and password you entered, then only reads: the API version, the list of agents, and each agent's network addresses, network interfaces and installed packages. It sends nothing else and never changes anything in Wazuh. The certificate must be one a public authority vouches for, or the one pinned when you pressed Save; if it changes, the pull stops before the password is sent, and you trust the new one only by typing the password again and pressing Save. Sent when you press Test or Save, and at the interval you chose.
14.to: Only the Wazuh server address you typed
14.control: Disconnect Wazuh in Inventory → Agents (the saved password is deleted), or turn off the agent intake module.

15.name: Outside view of your public IP (only when an administrator clicks it)
15.what: One of this box's own verified public IPs, in one HTTPS request to Shodan InternetDB, only when an administrator selects "Check what Shodan has seen" on that IP's page in External exposure and then confirms that the IP is sent to Shodan. Nothing else is sent: no key, no account, no other data of yours. Shodan sees the box's IP address and learns that someone asked about that IP. Only an IP the box has verified and still goes out through is sent: before it is sent, the box may first re-check its public IP (flow 9). At most once a minute; every request is in the audit log. Nothing runs on a schedule or in the background.
15.control: It is off until an administrator clicks: if nobody clicks, nothing is sent. Turn off the External exposure module to remove the button.

16.name: OpenVAS feed and images (only when you enable OpenVAS)
16.what: Vedette's system helper vedette-host has this box's container engine download the OpenVAS container images (Greenbone Community Edition, free; not the paid Greenbone Enterprise) and the Greenbone Community Feed (the vulnerability tests, the notus advisories, the scan configurations and the report formats, which Greenbone ships as images too; not its SCAP and CERT data, which Vedette does not use) from Greenbone's registry when an administrator enables the optional deep scan in External exposure, then once a week while it stays enabled (Vedette's feed update: those four feed data images only, never during a scan), and again when a Vedette update pins newer OpenVAS images. The first time, it also installs the distribution's docker-compose package from this box's own package sources, as an OS update does. The requests carry what any container client sends: the image name, its tag or digest and the architecture of this machine. The registry sees the box's IP address. Nothing of yours is sent: no target, no result, no Vedette data.
16.to: registry.community.greenbone.net (Greenbone AG's community container registry), and the box's own Debian or Ubuntu package mirrors for docker-compose. No Vedette-run server
16.control: It is off until an administrator enables OpenVAS (External exposure, Optional deep scan); turning OpenVAS off there stops its containers and the weekly feed update, so nothing more is downloaded. Turning off the External exposure module stops OpenVAS's containers too; they start again when the module is turned on while OpenVAS is enabled.

mirrorNote.bodyInfo: Mirror port traffic stays on the box. When a card of the box listens on a mirror (SPAN) port, the sensor reads only the names your devices look up (DNS), the server names of their TLS connections, the hosts of their web requests and the public addresses they open connections to, never the content of the traffic. The box compares these with the threat feeds it already holds and keeps only the matches (shown in Logs as bad connections, kept as long as the logs); everything that matches nothing is dropped at once. None of it leaves the box, except the matches you choose to forward to your own SIEM (flow 7) or that reach your alert channels as incidents (flow 5).

backup.desc: Give the file a password: it then also carries the decryption key, so a new box gets the saved secrets back, and a copy left on a laptop or a share gives nothing away.
backup.info: Settings, users (with their password hashes, never the passwords themselves), modules, devices, findings and the log. The hashes could be attacked offline.

ask.title: Download backup
ask.body: The box makes a new backup and saves it on your computer.
ask.protect: Protect the file with a password (recommended)
ask.passwordHint: At least 12 characters. A sentence of a few unrelated words is strong and easy to remember.
ask.short: The backup password needs at least 12 characters.
ask.mismatch: The two passwords are not the same.
ask.lostTitle: A lost password cannot be recovered
ask.lost: Nobody can open the file without it, not Vedette and not this box. Keep the password in a password manager, apart from the file.
ask.carriesKey: The password also protects the decryption key, which the file carries: on a new box every saved secret (AI and feed keys, alert channel passwords, tokens) and two-step sign-in come back, with no separate key file.
ask.how: Restoring the file on a new box asks for this password. The file uses the open age format, so the age tool (age -d) also opens it on any computer.

key.title: Keep the decryption key apart
key.desc: Without it, a backup downloaded without a password loses the saved secrets on another box.
key.descInfo: A backup downloaded without a password has no decryption key. On another box it brings back your devices, findings, users and settings, but not the saved secrets (AI and feed keys, alert channel passwords, tokens), and users with two-step sign-in cannot sign in. Download the key once and keep it somewhere other than your backups, like an emergency kit: with both files a new box comes back whole. A backup downloaded with a password already carries the key, protected by that password.
key.sso: Single sign-on accounts cannot confirm this download.
key.ssoInfo: You sign in with single sign-on, so there is no Vedette password to confirm this download with. An administrator who signs in with a password can download the key.
key.saved: Saved {{file}}. Keep it apart from your backups: whoever has both can read the saved secrets.

ask.title: Download the decryption key?
ask.body: Anyone with this key and a backup can read the saved secrets.
ask.info: Keep it offline, away from the backups. The download is recorded in the audit log.
ask.codeEmail: Click Download once to get a code by email, then type it here and click again.

restore.title: Backups on this box
restore.desc: Restoring a copy puts the box's data back to that moment.
restore.info: Copies the operating system helper keeps on the box: the ones you made and the ones the box takes by itself before an operating system install, a Vedette update or a restore.
restore.empty: No backups on this box yet.
restore.keyLine: Decryption key: every backup restores whole on this box; it matters only on another box.
restore.keyExplained: This box keeps its own key, so any backup restores whole here. On another box, a backup without the key brings back devices, findings, users and settings, but not the saved secrets (AI and feed keys, alert channel passwords, tokens), and users with two-step sign-in cannot sign in. A backup you downloaded with a password carries the key inside the file; for one downloaded without, download the key above to keep that option.

ask.title: Restore the backup from {{when}}?
ask.lost: Everything written since then is replaced: devices, findings, alerts, logs, the audit log, users and settings.
ask.kept: Before it restores, the box keeps a copy of the data it has now, listed here as Before restore, so you can go back. The audit log goes back too: lines written after this backup stay only in that copy.
ask.restart: Vedette restarts during the restore and the traps stop for about a minute; this page reconnects by itself.
ask.understand: I understand that data written since this backup is replaced

file.info: Use this when the backup you need is not in the list on this box, for example a file you kept elsewhere. A backup downloaded with a password asks for that password. A backup of this box, or one downloaded with a password, brings its saved secrets back; for a backup of another box downloaded without a password, add that box's decryption key file.

updates.title: Update Vedette
updates.desc: You update Vedette on the machine that runs it.

They do not move you to a new release: the image digests are fixed in vedette.env. When a release is offered, this page shows its steps; they are also in docs/INSTALL-CONTAINER.md section 5. If you run the sensors or syslog too, add {{files}} after --env-file vedette.env in both commands (leave out the add-on you do not run).

updates.notYet: No release information yet: no update check has run.
updates.notYetInfo: Vedette checks a few minutes after setup or a restart, then every 6 hours.
updates.notYetFailed: No release information yet: no update check has succeeded.

updates.runningUnknown: This machine's version is not known.

updates.stepKeep: Move the four files you run now into {{kept}}: that is the way back.
updates.stepKeepInfo: Do it in the folder of compose.yaml; the new folder is named after the version they run. An update replaces all four; your own settings are the two lines of vedette.env. mkdir refuses a folder that is already there, so nothing kept is overwritten.
updates.keptThere: If {{kept}} is already there, put its files back and rename it first:
updates.keptThereInfo: That happens after an update you stopped, or a way back you took. Then run this step again.
updates.keepLabel: Keep the files you run now
updates.stepFetch: Download the four files of Vedette {{version}} and their signatures:
updates.stepFetchInfo: They come from its release page, into this folder. The loop stops at the first file that fails.
updates.stepVerify: Check each signature: every line must print "<file> ok". At the first FAILED, stop:
updates.stepVerifyInfo: Use the vedette.pub you kept from the install (in this folder, not one taken from the release page). The signed comment of each file must name that file and version {{version}}.
updates.matchLabel: Check that vedette.env names these images
updates.pullLabel: Pull the new images and start them
updates.failStop: If any check fails, stop and put your files back.

updates.backOfferInfo: Putting your files back is also the way back after the update. If you run the sensors or syslog too, add {{files}} after --env-file vedette.env (leave out the add-on you do not run). Read the release notes before you update.
updates.backLabel: Put the files of {{kept}} back and start them

updates.verifyWhyInfo: This checks that each image is the one the Vedette project signed. Use the cosign.pub you kept from the install.
updates.verifyLabel: One line per image, by the digest in the signed release information
updates.matchWhy_one: Check that the new vedette.env names this image; it must print {{count}}, or do not go on:
updates.matchWhy_other: Check that the new vedette.env names these same images; it must print {{count}}, or do not go on:
updates.stepLines: Copy VEDETTE_BIND_IP and VEDETTE_HOSTS from {{kept}}/vedette.env into the new vedette.env:
updates.stepLinesInfo: A release leaves those two lines empty. Then pull the new images and start them. If you run the sensors or syslog too, add {{files}} after --env-file vedette.env in both commands (leave out the add-on you do not run).

network.desc: Set up this machine's network and the sensor with its own tools.
network.descInfo: Prepare the SPAN card on this machine yourself (promiscuous, no address), start the sensor with compose.sensors.yaml, then choose the card under Sensors. The address, extra IP and time server of the machine are set with its own tools.
network.descNoSpanInfo: Start the sensor with compose.sensors.yaml, then choose the card it listens on under Sensors. The address, extra IP and time server of the machine are set with its own tools.
